Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette:
Kofi Mensah is a 77-year-old African American man who has been married for more than five decades and has spent much of his working life as a software engineer. When he first arrived in the United States as a refugee, he carried with him the memory of fleeing in circumstances that still come back to him now in fragments rather than a full story. He does not describe the event as a continuous sequence so much as a set of frozen pictures: a moment of hurried movement, a face turned toward him in alarm, a scene of confusion and urgency, and then another image with no bridge between them. At times he can tell what happened, but the telling feels remote and oddly impersonal, as if he is recounting something that happened to a stranger. What remains most vivid to him are visual impressions - flashes that arrive in his mind without warning and then disappear just as quickly - while the feelings that should belong to the memory often seem missing, leaving him numb and disconnected from his own recollection.

Over the years, certain situations began to bring those images back with particular force. What unsettles Kofi most is being given orders or instructions, especially when they come in a sharp or unquestioning tone. A simple directive can make him feel as though he is no longer in the present moment but back in the atmosphere of threat and urgency that marked his flight. He also reacts to anything that reminds him of the refugee period itself, whether it is a news item, a conversation, or a scene that carries even a distant resemblance to those earlier events. At such moments he may notice the first signs of detachment - a sensation that he is beginning to feel unreal or cut off from the room around him - and that feeling is frightening to him because it signals that the old experience is near. He has come to watch for it carefully, taking it as a sign that he needs to get away before the sensation deepens.

In daily life, Kofi has gradually organized his world around staying away from situations that might set off those reactions. He avoids going out unless it feels absolutely necessary, and he makes a point of avoiding other people whenever he can. This has affected the rhythm of his days and narrowed the amount of contact he has with the outside world. Even ordinary errands can feel like something to endure rather than a routine part of life, because he never knows when he might encounter an instruction, a reminder, or a moment that leaves him drifting from the present. At home, he often keeps his mind occupied all the time, filling the hours with tasks or mental effort so there is less room for his thoughts to wander toward the past. In this way he has tried to prevent himself from becoming absorbed by the images that can surface when things are quiet. His wife has noticed that he is less likely to join family activities or spend time lingering with others, and that his world seems to have become smaller and more controlled.

As a software engineer, Kofi has remained capable and careful in his work, but even there the same sensitivities have had consequences. In a profession that often involves collaboration, requests, and directives, he can feel tense when others speak to him in a commanding way or expect an immediate response. He has learned to focus intensely on the technical details in front of him so that he can keep his attention occupied and avoid drifting into the detached state that worries him. He does best when he can work quietly and alone, with minimal interruption. The discipline that once served him well in his career has, over time, also become part of the effort he makes to keep his mind busy enough not to encounter the memories that arrive as pictures.

Kofi sought help because he recognized that his life had become increasingly constrained by these patterns. At 77, he is no longer willing to let his days revolve around staying inside, staying away from people, and keeping himself mentally occupied from morning to night just to avoid a moment of unreality or an unwanted picture from the past. He does not ask for his memories to vanish, but he hopes for some way to feel less threatened by them and less at the mercy of commands, reminders, and sudden detachment. What frightens him most is the sense that he could slip back into that old helplessness without warning; what he wants most is to be able to move through his home, his work, and the outside world with a steadier feeling that he is here now, not back in the refugee past.
